title: Extension methods and C# 14 members (adding behavior without editing types)
hook: Extension methods let you call static helper methods as if they were instance methods on a type you do not own. C# 14 adds extension properties and static-looking members on types — still compiled as static calls under the hood.

blocks.text: An **extension method** is a static method in a non-nested, non-generic static class whose first parameter is marked **this**. Callers write instance syntax; the compiler emits a static call. Language-Integrated Query (LINQ) `Where` and `Select` are the canonical example. **C# 14** adds **extension member blocks** that can declare instance-like properties and static members on a type — including operators — without modifying the original type's source.

entries.plainDefinition: A static method with a this first parameter, invoked with instance syntax.
A block inside a static class declaring extension(Receiver) { members } for instance-like or static members.
Real instance members on the type always win over extensions with the same signature.
entries.example: If string already has a method Foo, your extension Foo is ignored.

blocks.text: Extensions let you add domain-specific helpers to framework types without forking them. A Redis cache-key helper reads naturally as `id.AttemptCacheKey` instead of a static utility class. They never pierce encapsulation — private members stay inaccessible. Prefer real type members when you own the source; use extensions for cross-cutting layer behavior. C# 14 extension properties are interview-relevant: they compile to static methods but look like instance API.

blocks.title: Import the namespace
blocks.body: Extensions appear only after a using directive imports the namespace that holds the static class. They are not discovered by class name alone.

items.body: value.Helper(args) looks like an instance call.

items.title: Compiler checks instance members first
items.body: If the type defines a matching member, that wins. Extensions are fallback only.

items.title: Emit static call
items.body: Intermediate Language (IL) is identical to ClassName.Helper(value, args). No runtime patching of the type.

blocks.title: Extensions vs JS prototype patching vs TS augmentation
rows: Static calls only; type is not patched
Assigning Array.prototype.foo changes every array globally
TS module augmentation adds types; JS has no compile guard
TS can declare methods on interfaces; implementation is still manual
Cannot access private members of extended type
Prototype code can sometimes reach closures if you control the module

blocks.title: Expecting an extension to override a type method
blocks.body: Instance members always win. An extension with the same name is silently ignored when a real member exists.

blocks.title: Mutating a struct through a by-value extension
blocks.body: Without ref on the receiver, struct extensions receive a copy. Changes do not flow back to the caller's local.

interviewTakeaways: this-methods: instance-looking static methods, methods only.
C# 14 extension { }: instance and static members, including properties and operators.
Both compile to static calls; real instance members always win.
ref receivers mutate structs; by-value receivers copy.
commonPitfalls: Expecting an extension to override a type's own method.
Forgetting using of the namespace so the member vanishes from IntelliSense.
Mutating a struct through a by-value extension and wondering why the local is unchanged.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript can assign Array.prototype.foo and change every array. C# extensions are compile-time sugar; they do not patch the type for other languages or reflection as instance members.
TypeScript can merge interfaces to add methods at the type level; implementation is still a runtime assignment. C# 14 extensions are implemented by the compiler as static members.
